by_day.deck_caption:
How to stay healthy at a desk job. 5 habits, backed by science.

If you sit most of the day, your job is not the problem. Sitting still is. These are the 5 things I'd do every single workday, and each one has real research behind it.

Sources:
1. Two-minute walks every 20 minutes of sitting cut the blood sugar response to a test drink from 6.9 to 5.2 in 19 overweight adults. Diabetes Care, 2012. doi:10.2337/dc11-1931
2. Across 1,005,791 people, about 60 to 75 minutes a day of moderate activity wiped out the extra risk of death tied to sitting 8+ hours. Lancet, 2016. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(16)30370-1
3. In 573 office workers, one hour a week of neck and shoulder strength training cut headache frequency and intensity by about 50%. Musculoskelet Sci Pract, 2018. doi:10.1016/j.msksp.2017.08.003
4. Office workers with more daylight at work slept longer and reported better sleep quality than workers in windowless spaces. J Clin Sleep Med, 2015. doi:10.5664/jcsm.3780
5. Reading on a light-emitting screen before bed made people slower to fall asleep, cut melatonin and delayed the body clock versus a printed book. PNAS, 2015. doi:10.1073/pnas.1418490112

The activity and daylight findings come from observational data, so they show a link, not proof. Still worth doing.

Save this for your next long day at the desk. And send it to the friend who works 9 hours without standing up once.

by_day.deck_caption:
Signs under-eating is killing your gains. And 6 ways to fix it.

More of a deficit isn't always better. Eat too little for too long and you stop building muscle, lose the muscle you have, feel cold and flat, and set up a rebound. Here's what the research shows.

Sources:
1. A meta-analysis of resistance training in an energy deficit: lean mass gains impaired, strength comparable, about 500 kcal a day deficit prevented lean mass gains. Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2022. doi:10.1111/sms.14075
2. Review of low energy availability in natural male bodybuilding: muscle loss over 40% of weight lost in case studies, body fat overshoot on refeeding. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab, 2017. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.2016-0332
3. 48 overweight adults, 6 months of 25% calorie restriction lowered core body temperature. JAMA, 2006. doi:10.1001/jama.295.13.1539
4. One natural bodybuilder over 12 months: testosterone fell from 9.22 to 2.27 ng/mL, mood disturbance rose from 6 to 43 in prep. Int J Sports Physiol Perform, 2013. doi:10.1123/ijspp.8.5.582
5. MATADOR, 36 men with obesity who finished: intermittent dieting lost more fat (12.3 vs 8.0 kg) and had a smaller drop in resting energy burn. Int J Obes, 2018. doi:10.1038/ijo.2017.206
6. 24 athletes lifting 4 days a week: losing 0.7% of body weight per week gained 2.1% lean mass, losing 1.4% per week did not. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab, 2011. doi:10.1123/ijsnem.21.2.97
7. 40 young men on a 40% deficit: 2.4 g protein per kg gained 1.2 kg lean mass vs 0.1 kg on 1.2 g per kg. Am J Clin Nutr, 2016. doi:10.3945/ajcn.115.119339
8. Natural bodybuilding prep review: 0.5 to 1% weekly loss, 2.3 to 3.1 g protein per kg of lean mass. J Int Soc Sports Nutr, 2014. doi:10.1186/1550-2783-11-20

Save this for the next time you think cutting harder is the answer. And send it to the friend who's been on 1,400 calories for two months and wonders why he looks softer.

by_day.reason: Muscle & hypertrophy is the fixed Wednesday theme; this week's topic was selected from carousel_topic_engine score 83.8. Signals: how to build muscle; hypertrophy training; muscle growth peptides; How do people survive on less than 1700 calories
by_day.reason_public: Muscle & hypertrophy is the fixed Wednesday theme. This week's angle comes from what people keep asking us: how to build muscle, hypertrophy training, muscle growth peptides.
by_day.drive_link: [Prepared deck in Drive — open when posting]
by_day.deck_caption:
Hours of cardio were never the point. 10 cardio findings.

10 peer-reviewed findings on what cardio really does for fat, muscle and life span (November 2026). No gurus, no bro-science. Every claim on the slides is cited below. Save it.

1. Any running beat none, even once a week
2. Fitness showed no ceiling on the benefit
3. Intervals bought the same fat loss in 40% less time
4. Running cut fat. Cycling did not
5. Short hard intervals did not melt more fat
6. Intervals did build fitness fast
7. Sedentary adults gained about 6 points of fitness
8. Lifting plus cardio still beat cardio alone for muscle
9. At the fiber level, running cost a little growth
10. Walking or jogging cut depression scores

What the research says:
- 232,149 adults across 6 cohorts: running went with 27% lower all cause mortality, and no weekly dose beat any other (HR 0.73).
- 122,007 treadmill tested adults: the fittest group had one fifth the risk of dying of the least fit group (HR 0.20).

Sources:
1. Any running beat none, with no dose trend: Pedisic 2020, Br J Sports Med. PMID 31685526.
2. Fitness had no upper limit of benefit: Mandsager 2018, JAMA Netw Open. PMID 30646252.
3. Intervals matched moderate cardio for fat loss in less time: Wewege 2017, Obes Rev. PMID 28401638.
4. Running cut fat mass, cycling did not: Wewege 2017, Obes Rev. PMID 28401638.
5. Low volume HIIT did not change fat mass: Sultana 2019, Sports Med. PMID 31401727.
6. Interval training raised VO2max: Bacon 2013, PLoS One. PMID 24066036.
7. HIIT raised fitness and trimmed waist in sedentary adults: Strauss 2026, Cochrane Database Syst Rev. PMID 41810896.
8. Concurrent training still built muscle, mostly with running as the cost: Wilson 2012, J Strength Cond Res. PMID 22002517.
9. Running had a small cost on type I fiber growth: Lundberg 2022, Sports Med. PMID 35476184.
10. Walking or jogging reduced depression scores: Noetel 2024, BMJ. PMID 38355154.

This is not an anti-cardio or pro-cardio post. Several of these are observational: running and fitness tracked with longer lives, they do not prove cardio caused it. Intervals were a time saver, not a fat loss shortcut.

Save this for your next cardio day. And send it to the lifter who skips cardio because he thinks it kills his gains.

by_day.drive_link: [Prepared deck in Drive — open when posting]
by_day.deck_caption:
Testosterone is not the muscle switch the ads sell. 10 findings.

10 peer-reviewed findings on testosterone, training and what actually moves it (November 2026). No gurus, no bro-science. Every claim on the slides is cited below. Save it.

1. The post workout hormone spike predicted nothing
2. Losing weight raised testosterone
3. A short night did not crash it. A missed night did
4. Low fat diets lowered it
5. Soy did not lower testosterone
6. Low testosterone needs symptoms, not just a number
7. Very high doses did build muscle. Normal levels were never the test
8. Replacing it matched placebo on heart events
9. Treatment cut diabetes risk, with a catch
10. A supplement moved the number, not the stress

What the research says:
- 49 resistance trained men, 12 weeks: no link between the acute post workout rise in any anabolic hormone and the change in strength or muscle.
- 24 studies: losing weight raised total testosterone, by 2.87 nmol/L on a low calorie diet and 8.73 after bariatric surgery.

Sources:
1. Post workout hormone rises did not predict gains: Morton 2016, J Appl Physiol. PMID 27174923.
2. Weight loss raised testosterone: Corona 2013, Eur J Endocrinol. PMID 23482592.
3. Total sleep loss lowered testosterone, partial did not: Su 2021, Sleep Med. PMID 34801825.
4. Low fat diets lowered testosterone: Whittaker 2021, J Steroid Biochem Mol Biol. PMID 33741447.
5. Soy did not change male hormones: Reed 2021, Reprod Toxicol. PMID 33383165.
6. Low testosterone was defined by symptoms plus a cutoff: Wu 2010, N Engl J Med. PMID 20554979.
7. Supraphysiologic doses built muscle, lifting added more: Bhasin 1996, N Engl J Med. PMID 8637535.
8. Testosterone therapy matched placebo on cardiac events: Lincoff 2023, N Engl J Med. PMID 37326322.
9. Testosterone cut diabetes risk, raised haematocrit: Wittert 2021, Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol. PMID 33338415.
10. Ashwagandha raised free testosterone, not stress relief: Smith 2023, J Psychopharmacol. PMID 37740662.

This is not an anti-testosterone post. Treatment helps men with a diagnosed deficiency. The point is that workout spikes and boosters are not what builds your muscle.

Save this for the next time an ad promises a hormone fix. And send it to the guy at your gym who buys testosterone boosters.

8. Testosterone therapy matched placebo on cardiac events: Lincoff 2023, N Engl J Med. PMID 37326322.

This is not an anti-testosterone post. Treatment helps men with a diagnosed deficiency. The point is that workout spikes and boosters are not what builds your muscle.

by_day.deck_caption:
Motivation never made anyone consistent. 10 findings.

10 peer-reviewed findings on what keeps people training (November 2026). No gurus, no bro-science. Every claim on the slides is cited below. Save it.

1. Wanting it more barely changed what people did
2. A when and where plan helped
3. Self-monitoring worked best with a feedback loop
4. A tracker added about 1,800 steps a day
5. Paying people worked, for a while
6. A habit took about two months, but ranged from 4 days to 335
7. How a session felt predicted whether people came back
8. Liking it beat forcing it, long term
9. Twice a week per muscle beat once a week
10. More days was not always better

What the research says:
- 11 randomised trials: raising intention moved behavior by only d 0.15, a third of the change in intention itself (d 0.45).
- 122 evaluations, 44,747 adults: self-monitoring plus a feedback loop reached an effect of 0.42, vs 0.26 for programs without it.

Sources:
1. Raising intention barely moved behavior: Rhodes 2012, Health Psychol. PMID 22390739.
2. If-then plans raised physical activity: Silva 2018, PLoS One. PMID 30427874.
3. Self-monitoring plus a feedback loop worked best: Michie 2009, Health Psychol. PMID 19916637.
4. Activity trackers added steps: Ferguson 2022, Lancet Digit Health. PMID 35868813.
5. Financial incentives raised attendance short term: Mitchell 2013, Am J Prev Med. PMID 24139781.
6. Habits took about two months with huge variation: Singh 2024, Healthcare. PMID 39685110.
7. Feeling good during exercise predicted future activity: Rhodes 2015, Ann Behav Med. PMID 25921307.
8. Intrinsic motivation predicted long term adherence: Teixeira 2012, Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. PMID 22726453.
9. Training a muscle twice a week beat once: Schoenfeld 2016, Sports Med. PMID 27102172.
10. Three to five sessions a week had the largest mental health link: Chekroud 2018, Lancet Psychiatry. PMID 30099000.

This is not an anti-motivation post. Several of these are observational, and effect sizes come from different reviews and measures. The point is that systems did more than a good mood.

Save this for the next time you fall off. And send it to the friend who restarts every Monday.

by_day.deck_caption:
10 longevity findings. Not one of them is about your weight.

10 peer-reviewed findings on what actually predicts a long life. No gurus, no bro-science. Every claim on the slides is cited below. Save it.

1. Being fit beat being thin
2. Low fitness carried the same risk as smoking
3. The fittest found no ceiling on the benefit
4. Grip strength predicted death better than blood pressure
5. A strong grip did not prevent falls or fractures
6. Strength counted even after cardio was accounted for
7. Lifting plus cardio tracked with the biggest drop
8. 40 push-ups marked the lowest heart risk
9. Needing your hands to get off the floor flagged higher risk
10. Failing a one-leg stand tracked with nearly double the risk

What the research says:
- 33 studies, 102,980 people: each 1 MET higher fitness, about 1 km/h faster running pace, went with 13% lower risk of dying (RR 0.87).
- 502,293 UK adults: every 5 kg lower grip carried HR 1.16 in men and 1.20 in women. Weakness meant a grip under 26 kg for men.

Sources:
1. Being fit beat being thin: Barry 2014, Prog Cardiovasc Dis. PMID 24438729.
2. Low fitness matched smoking, and no ceiling on the benefit: Mandsager 2018, JAMA Netw Open. PMID 30646252.
3. Grip beat blood pressure, but did not prevent falls: Leong 2015, Lancet. PMID 25982160.
4. Strength counted beyond cardio: Ruiz 2008, BMJ. PMID 18595904.
5. Lifting plus cardio: Saeidifard 2019, Eur J Prev Cardiol. PMID 31104484.
6. 40 push-ups: Yang 2019, JAMA Netw Open. PMID 30768197.
7. Sit and rise test: Brito 2014, Eur J Prev Cardiol. PMID 23242910.
8. 10 seconds on one leg: Araujo 2022, Br J Sports Med. PMID 35728834.
9. Each step up in fitness: Kodama 2009, JAMA. PMID 19454641.
10. Grip in 502,293 adults: Celis-Morales 2018, BMJ. PMID 29739772.

This isn't an anti weight loss post. These are mostly observational studies: fitness and strength tracked with a longer life, they do not prove training caused it. I still bet on training.

what_to_record.intro: Research awaiting an update (public questions: last available 2026-10-23). Suggestions use the last available material or the recurring content schedule. Shot requests tied to this week's themes. Carousel days ask for a set of situations with a count and a real place, because a deck needs its own footage. Shoot them as they happen in a normal day, not as a studio set. 37 shots in total this week.

assets.where: Sat down, menu open, plate arriving. Phone at chest height, no flatlay staging
assets.why: The 'eating out ruins it' objection is the most common one in the DMs and we have no footage of it.

assets.where: Ordering, or the bag on the passenger seat
assets.why: Covers the weeknight version of the same objection.

assets.where: Weighing something ordinary like rice or peanut butter, hands in frame
assets.why: Makes a deficit look like a small habit instead of a diet.

assets.where: Fridge open after dinner, or standing at the counter with a snack
assets.why: Evening eating is where most weeks actually break.

assets.where: Office, laptop, car, or workday transition; quick walk/stretch/check-in
assets.why: Matches busy-life/remote-work demand from the audience.
assets.source_theme: Modern life: remote work, screens, AI & health

assets.where: Mid set on a main lift. One from the side, one from the front, one close on the grip, one of the rack or plates
assets.why: Body slides currently reuse the cover image; a deck needs its own angles.

assets.what: 2 shots: the correct rep vs the common mistake
assets.where: Same exercise, same angle, filmed back to back
assets.why: The single most reusable teaching visual we do not have.

assets.where: Writing or typing the set down, gym in the background
assets.why: Makes progressive overload visible instead of abstract.

assets.where: Sat on the bench, breathing, checking the clock
assets.why: Real gym texture for filler slides.

assets.where: Home or office; stretching, walk, sleep wind-down, massage gun, or caffeine cutoff
assets.why: Answers recovery questions with a repeatable visual routine.

assets.where: Kitchen counter, store aisle, or cabinet; show what is useful vs skippable
assets.why: Supports Friday supplement Q&A without sounding like a sales pitch.

assets.where: Two similar products held side by side, label readable. Dairy, bread, sauces, snacks
assets.why: Label comparisons are the most saved format and we reuse the same two photos.

assets.where: Half full, real shop, not a styled haul
assets.why: Grounds the advice in a normal weekly shop.

assets.where: Overhead and at eye level, at a real table
assets.why: Lets a slide show a portion instead of describing it.

assets.what: 2 shots: the lunchbox or prep container
assets.where: Being filled, or open at a desk
assets.why: Covers the prep question without a full meal-prep set.

assets.where: Phone with the message thread open, or a call on a laptop. No client faces or names on screen
assets.why: The proof post needs a picture of the process, not a transformation photo.

assets.where: Writing an adjustment, editing the app, crossing something out
assets.why: Shows the coaching, which is the part being sold.
